config.title: Build typed registry with key constraints

intro.title: Build typed registry with key constraints
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a typed registry that stores and retrieves values using specific keys, ensuring type safety throughout. You will learn how to use TypeScript's generic types and key constraints to define which keys are allowed in the registry. The main technologies involved are TypeScript interfaces, generics, and union types for restricting keys. By the end, you'll have a functional registry that prevents invalid keys at compile time, reinforcing type-safe data structures.
intro.usecase: A typed registry with key constraints is a foundational pattern for managing dynamic, type-safe collections in real-world applications. For example, in a dashboard builder, you might have a registry of available widgets (like charts, tables, or metrics) where each widget type is registered under a unique key, ensuring that only valid, pre-defined components can be instantiated. This pattern is also essential in plugin systems, such as a code editor's extension marketplace, where extensions must be registered with specific identifiers to prevent conflicts and enable safe, predictable loading. By enforcing these constraints, developers can build scalable, maintainable systems that prevent runtime errors and improve developer experience.

objectives: Construct a typed registry interface with generic constraints
Implement a registry class that enforces key-value type relationships
Apply TypeScript's keyof and mapped types to constrain registry operations
Configure type-safe methods for adding and retrieving registry entries
Manipulate the registry with compile-time validation of key constraints
Initialize a registry instance with properly typed initial data
Integrate the typed registry into a simple demonstration module

steps.title: Import TypeScript utilities for type constraints
steps.instruction: In the TypeScript file, add a comment indicating that we'll use TypeScript's built-in keyof and Record utilities for type constraints.
steps.hint: You don't need to import anything from modules. Just write a comment explaining what utilities we'll use.
steps.analogousExample: // We'll use TypeScript's built-in utilities like keyof and Record
steps.seedCode: // We'll use TypeScript's built-in utilities like keyof and Record
steps.expectedOutcome: A comment is added to indicate we'll use keyof and Record utilities for type constraints.
successCriteria: The comment mentions keyof and Record utilities.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure your comment mentions both keyof and Record utilities.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add a comment indicating we'll use TypeScript's keyof and Record utilities.

steps.title: Define the allowed keys type using string literal union
steps.instruction: Create a type called AllowedKeys that defines a union of string literal values: 'user', 'product', and 'order'.
steps.hint: Use the TypeScript syntax: type AllowedKeys = 'user' | 'product' | 'order';
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: a union type for allowed colors
type AllowedColors = 'red' | 'green' | 'blue';
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a type AllowedKeys that restricts keys to only 'user', 'product', or 'order'.
successCriteria: The AllowedKeys type is defined as a union of the three string literals: 'user', 'product', 'order'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure AllowedKeys includes exactly 'user', 'product', and 'order' as string literals.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match the required type definition. Try creating a type AllowedKeys with the three specific string values.

steps.title: Define the value type for registry entries
steps.instruction: Create an interface called RegistryValue that defines the shape of data that will be stored in your registry. It should have id (string), name (string), and timestamp (Date) properties.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with their types.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a RegistryValue interface that specifies the structure of values in your typed registry.
successCriteria: RegistryValue interface is defined with id: string, name: string, and timestamp: Date properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your interface includes all three required properties with the correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. Create an interface named RegistryValue with id (string), name (string), and timestamp (Date) properties.

steps.title: Create the typed registry interface using Record
steps.instruction: Create a type called TypedRegistry that uses TypeScript's Record utility type to map AllowedKeys to RegistryValue.
steps.hint: Use Record<Keys, Value> where Keys is AllowedKeys and Value is RegistryValue.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a TypedRegistry type that ensures only valid AllowedKeys can map to RegistryValue entries.
successCriteria: A type named TypedRegistry is defined using Record<AllowedKeys, RegistryValue>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using Record with AllowedKeys and RegistryValue.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you defined a type called TypedRegistry using Record<AllowedKeys, RegistryValue>.

steps.title: Initialize an empty registry object with the correct type
steps.instruction: Create a constant called 'registry' and initialize it as an empty object, explicitly typing it as 'TypedRegistry'.
steps.hint: Use the 'const' keyword, the name 'registry', and assign it an empty object '{}' with the type annotation ': TypedRegistry'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: typed empty object
const emptyConfig: Record<string, number> = {};
steps.expectedOutcome: A constant 'registry' is created with the type 'TypedRegistry' and initialized as an empty object.
successCriteria: The constant 'registry' is declared, typed as 'TypedRegistry', and assigned an empty object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've declared a constant named 'registry', typed it as 'TypedRegistry', and assigned it an empty object '{}'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The registry constant is missing or incorrectly typed. Remember to create 'const registry: TypedRegistry = {};'.

steps.title: Create a function to add entries with type checking
steps.instruction: Create a function named addToRegistry that takes two parameters: key (of type AllowedKeys) and value (of type RegistryValue), and adds them to the registry object.
steps.hint: Define a function that accepts the typed parameters and assigns the value to the registry object using the key as the property name.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named addToRegistry is defined with proper TypeScript parameter types that will enable type-safe addition to the registry.
successCriteria: The addToRegistry function is created with two typed parameters (key: AllowedKeys, value: RegistryValue) and contains logic to assign the value to the registry object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the function, but make sure it has both typed parameters and the assignment logic to add to the registry.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't properly defined. Check that you've named it addToRegistry, given it the correct parameter types, and included the assignment to the registry.

steps.title: Create a function to retrieve entries with proper return type
steps.instruction: Create a function named getFromRegistry that accepts a key parameter of type AllowedKeys and returns the corresponding RegistryValue or undefined if the key doesn't exist in the registry.
steps.hint: The function should check if the key exists in the registry object and return the value if found, otherwise return undefined.
steps.expectedOutcome: A type-safe retrieval function that properly handles missing keys by returning undefined.
successCriteria: The getFromRegistry function exists, accepts a key of type AllowedKeys, and returns RegistryValue | undefined.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function accepts a key of type AllowedKeys and returns RegistryValue | undefined.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't match the requirements. It should accept a key of type AllowedKeys and return RegistryValue | undefined.

steps.title: Test adding valid entries to the registry
steps.instruction: Call the addToRegistry function with a valid AllowedKeys value and a properly structured RegistryValue object to populate the registry.
steps.hint: Use one of the allowed keys from your AllowedKeys type and provide an object matching the RegistryValue interface structure.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of calling a typed function with valid arguments
addToRegistry('key1', { label: 'Item 1', value: 100 });
steps.expectedOutcome: The registry should contain the added entry with proper type checking enforced by TypeScript.
successCriteria: addToRegistry is called with a valid AllowedKeys value and a RegistryValue object that matches the interface structure.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using a valid key from your AllowedKeys type and providing a complete RegistryValue object with all required properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The call to addToRegistry doesn't match the expected signature. Check that you're using a valid AllowedKeys value and providing a properly structured RegistryValue object.

steps.title: Test retrieving entries from the registry
steps.instruction: Call the getFromRegistry function with a valid key to retrieve a value and store it in a variable.
steps.hint: Use the getFromRegistry function you created earlier, passing one of the allowed keys you used when adding entries.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: retrieving a value from a typed map
const retrievedValue = myMap.get('validKey');
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a variable containing the typed value retrieved from the registry using a valid key.
successCriteria: The getFromRegistry function is called with a valid key and the result is stored in a variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling getFromRegistry with one of the allowed keys and storing the result.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try calling the getFromRegistry function with a valid key like 'user' or 'product' and assign the result to a variable.

steps.title: Demonstrate type safety by attempting invalid operations
steps.instruction: Add a line that attempts to add an entry with an invalid key (like 'category') to the registry using the addToRegistry function.
steps.hint: Try calling addToRegistry with a key that isn't in the AllowedKeys union type. TypeScript should show a compile-time error.
steps.analogousExample:
// Attempting to use an invalid key
addToRegistry('invalidKey', { id: 999, name: 'Test' });
steps.expectedOutcome: TypeScript will show a compile-time error because 'category' is not a valid AllowedKeys type, demonstrating how the type system prevents invalid key usage.
successCriteria: The code includes an attempt to call addToRegistry with an invalid key like 'category'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling addToRegistry with a key that isn't in the AllowedKeys union type.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try calling addToRegistry with a key that isn't 'user', 'product', or 'order' to see TypeScript's type safety in action.
